title: GS/OS was Apple’s Colorful Desktop That Lived on the Wrong Machine from the 1980s - TechEBlog -
content: Most people who remember personal computers from the late 1980s think first of the Macintosh and its clean black-and-white interface. Apple had already shipped something that looked and behaved a lot like it, only this version ran in color on a machine that still carried the Apple II name. That system was GS/OS, and it arrived in 1988 as the heart of Apple IIGS System Software 4.0. GS/OS was built from the start in 100% 16-bit code for the 65816 CPU inside the IIGS, which was a significant shift from previous versions. Most other software on this computer was still inadequately optimized for 8-bit routines carried over from the previous Apple II generation. The improved code resulted in significantly faster disk access, screen rendering, and program loading. Customers who had upgraded from ProDOS 16 were particularly affected. title: If BMW Brings Back the F 650 GS, It's Reviving the Bike That Made Budget Adventure Riding Mainstream - Top Speed
content: Spy shots published this week show BMW testing an all-new middleweight adventure prototype that appears to slot directly between the F 450 GS and F 900 GS — a gap that has existed in the lineup for years. The prototype rolls on 21-inch front and 18-inch rear cross-spoke wheels, uses a steel bridge frame closely related to the F 900 GS, and carries a parallel-twin engine with visible kinship to the F 450 GS's powerplant. Whether it arrives as an F 600 GS, F 650 GS, or F 700 GS, the nameplate question alone is enough to get adventure riders talking. For many in the community, the F 650 GS badge carries real weight. The F 650 GS Dakar from the early 2000s remains a benchmark for what an accessible, genuinely capable adventure bike can be — the kind of machine that introduced a generation of riders to long-distance dirt travel before the segment exploded into what it is today. BMW returning to that territory, with a modern platform and the resources of the GS family behind it, would be a significant moment for the middleweight adventure market. The prototype is clearly a mix of components drawn from across BMW's existing GS range. The chassis and braking system lean toward the F 900 GS, while the rear shock mounting and swingarm design echo the smaller F 450 GS. Ground clearance looks generous — observers estimate around 230 millimeters (roughly nine inches) of suspension travel — and the wheel sizes confirm this is built with genuine off-road intent, not just the appearance of it. Kerb weight is reported to be around 204 kilograms (approximately 450 pounds), placing it neatly between the F 450 GS and F 900 GS on the scales as well as in the lineup. The headlight already shows a finished X-shaped design borrowed from the R 1300 GS, though the characteristic GS beak is absent — likely a sign that front-end bodywork is still in progress. The overall proportions draw comparisons to the Yamaha Ténéré 700, which is no accident: both the Ténéré 700 and the Honda XL750 Transalp are reportedly being used as development benchmarks during testing. The powertrain is where things get genuinely complicated. The engine is a parallel twin with clear ties to the F 450 GS platform, but how heavily BMW reworks it — or whether it builds something new entirely — remains open. The most concrete reference point is the Norton Atlas, where BMW partner TVS uses a 585cc version of a reworked parallel twin producing 70 hp. That engine is regarded as a plausible starting point, though the prototype's motor differs from the Norton unit in several visible areas. There's also a technical wrinkle worth noting: the F 450 GS runs an unusual 135-degree crankpin offset, while the Norton twin uses the more conventional 270-degree firing interval common in this class. That difference affects how the engine feels under throttle and how well power can be metered on loose surfaces — exactly the conditions this bike is being built for. Whether BMW carries its unconventional setup into the middleweight or switches to the standard layout is one of the more interesting unanswered questions surrounding the project. Power output is expected to land somewhere in the 65–80 hp range, keeping it well clear of the F 900 GS's 105 hp. The middleweight adventure segment has changed dramatically since the original F 650 GS era. The Yamaha Ténéré 700 and KTM 690 Adventure have set a high bar for off-road performance at accessible price points, while the Royal Enfield Himalayan and Honda NX500 have pushed the entry point lower still. It's a crowded, competitive space — and it's one BMW has been absent from for long enough that the Ténéré 700 and Transalp have had time to build loyal followings. A new middleweight GS, priced between the F 450 GS and F 900 GS, would give BMW a genuine answer to all of them. One estimate places the India price around 1.2 million rupees (roughly $12,500 USD), though that figure carries no manufacturer backing. What's clear is that BMW's intent is to compete on capability first — the 21-inch front wheel, long-travel suspension, and F 900 GS-derived braking all point to a machine that takes off-road performance seriously rather than treating it as a styling exercise. A production launch is not expected before 2028, and the unfinished state of the prototype confirms there's significant development work still ahead. EICMA 2026 is the earliest realistic opportunity for an official reveal, though even that isn't confirmed. For riders shopping the middleweight segment right now, the prototype is a signal worth paying attention to — BMW is coming, and it's building something that looks like it means business. title: FOR SALE: 1957 Porsche 356 A Carrera 1500 GS Coupe by Reutter - Sports Car Digest
content: One of the most desirable and historically significant variants of the early 356 Now offered for sale through RM Sotheby’s Private Sales, this 1957 Porsche 356 A Carrera 1500 GS Coupe by Reutter represents one of the most desirable and historically significant variants of the early 356. Sold new to a U.S. Air Force serviceman stationed in Japan and equipped with sought-after Rudge wheels, the car combines exceptional rarity with an important place in Porsche’s performance-car lineage. The Carrera name was introduced in response to Porsche’s growing success with the 550 Spyder in the demanding Carrera Panamericana. To bring some of the Spyder’s competition-bred character to the road, Porsche adapted a detuned version of Ernst Fuhrmann’s sophisticated 1.5-liter, four-cam, twin-spark racing engine for a limited-production version of the 356 A. Unveiled at the 1955 Frankfurt Motor Show for the 1956 model year, the Carrera established a designation that would ultimately become synonymous with Porsche’s highest-performance road cars. The Fuhrmann-designed engine was available across the 356 A Coupe, Cabriolet, and Speedster ranges. Its advanced construction included roller-bearing crankshaft technology, a dry-sump lubrication system, chrome-plated cylinder bores, and an 8.1:1 compression ratio. Power was delivered through Porsche’s improved Type 644 four-speed transmission, while the dry-sump oil tank was positioned within the left-rear fender well and protected by a mesh screen bearing the car’s chassis number. Twin Autopulse fuel pumps and a pressure-regulating valve completed the specialized fuel system. Porsche also enhanced the Carrera’s chassis to complement its increased performance. Revised torsion bars, larger shock absorbers, and updated suspension bump stops improved both handling and road manners. The Carrera adopted 15-inch wheels rather than the 16-inch units used on earlier Pre-A models, while wheel width increased to 4.25 inches. Originally finished in Ivory with sealed-beam headlights and dual exterior mirrors, this example was delivered in January 1957 to Harold W. Kuhns, a U.S. Air Force captain stationed in Japan, through Mitsuwa Motors of Tokyo. It later returned to the United States, reportedly accompanying Kuhns to New York, before passing through several owners in Colorado and New Hampshire. The Porsche was subsequently exported to Germany before being acquired by its consignor in 2017 and brought back to the United States. It has remained in Southern California since. The Carrera 1500 GS earned its reputation through a combination of sophisticated engineering, competitive performance, exceptional handling, and limited production. Successful in competition and highly prized by collectors, the model remains among the most coveted of all 356 variants. This example therefore offers an uncommon opportunity to acquire a significant piece of Porsche history—one that helped establish the Carrera name as a benchmark for performance.
